articles.title: Cruz rips ‘right-wing socialism,’ says GOP shouldn’t be ‘giving away free stuff’
articles.summary: GOP Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) on Tuesday criticized populist Republicans for proposing “right-wing socialism,” arguing the strategy will not pay off for the part...
articles.body:
GOP Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) on Tuesday criticized populist Republicans for proposing "right-wing socialism," arguing the strategy will not pay off for the party.

"I consider myself very much a populist, Cruz said on Fox News's "The Will Cain Show," claiming "the base that has elected me every time has been blue-collar workers."

"Here's the difference: the way to be a populist is not get in the [Sen.] Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) game of giving away free stuff," the Texas senator told host Will Cain. "The way to be a populist is fight for the jobs of working men and women, fight for small businesses."

Earlier this month, President Trump proposed to send every American adult a $5,000 dividend if Republicans hold on to control of Congress in November. But multiple GOP lawmakers, including senators , have criticized the proposal, noting it would add to the $40-plus trillion national debt .

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), on the other hand, has said he will prepare legislation to send those dividends to roughly 270 million Americans should the GOP hold serve in the House and Senate. If the federal government sends a check to every adult, the initiative's price tag will exceed $1 trillion.

Cruz on Tuesday criticized Democrats for the crop of democratic socialists winning primaries across the country, and urged Republicans to avoid following their lead.

"There are two answers to 'right-wing socialism': no, and hell no," Cruz wrote on social platform X , arguing that socialism "has been a train wreck" everywhere it has been implemented.

"There are misguided voices in MAGA saying, 'Let's embrace socialism lite,'" the former presidential candidate told Cain. "You know what? If we campaign and say, 'We'll be just like the Democrats except not as a generous Santa Claus,' that's a path to losing."

articles.title: ‘Don't owe the old guys anything’: Backlash builds to GOP chairs clinging to power
articles.summary: A behind-the-scenes battle is playing out over several powerful House Republicans who don’t want to be forced out of their plum posts.
articles.body:
House Republicans for decades have prided themselves on their strict three-term limit for committee leaders, saying it promotes fresh blood in the party ranks.

But that limit has grown less strict in recent years, and a growing number of GOP lawmakers are aching for a crackdown.

Three of the 20 sitting House chairs have signaled interest in applying for a waiver to bypass the six-year term limit Republicans have had in place for more than 30 years. If each follows through, it would be the first time so many exceptions have been sought at once — and some Republicans are openly warning the practice is spinning out of control.

"We have term limits for a reason," House Appropriations Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) said in an interview.

The question will be in the hands of the House Republican Steering Committee , a 35-member body representing a cross-section of the larger GOP conference. Depending on the outcome of the midterms — and the subsequent GOP leadership elections — the influential panel could also see an influx of younger members who might be even less inclined to give longtime committee leaders a two-year extension.

"They don't owe the old guys anything," Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.) said in an interview. "They don't see seniority as the main thing anymore, because even leadership is pretty young. So this is a whole new generation."

The up-or-out dynamic has long been a point of distinction inside the House GOP, where generational resentments have been much more muted than among Democrats — who have no committee term limits and have seen younger members chafe as veterans spend a decade or more occupying top panel spots.

This year, however, both Agriculture Chair G.T. Thompson of Pennsylvania and Armed Services Chair Mike Rogers of Alabama have said they intend to seek waivers after leading their respective committees for six years already. So, too, has Rep. Ken Calvert of California, who chairs the powerful Appropriations subcommittee on Defense and is already serving a fourth term under a waiver. Natural Resources Chair Bruce Westerman of Arkansas has also signaled he might seek an exception.

As the chairs line up to make their case to the Steering Committee, many of its current members are publicly voicing their opposition to watering down the term limits rule, which dates to 1992 under the leadership of then-future Speaker Newt Gingrich.

"I would say waivers are rare and will remain so," said Rep. Ryan Zinke (R-Mont.), a Steering member. "There's also a lot of talent that has been waiting."

"There's a reason we have term limits — they work," said Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.), another Steering member who is challenging Thompson for the Agriculture spot.

At least one top GOP leader is sending similar signals: Majority Whip Tom Emmer said in a recent interview he's "not a fan" of the waiver practice , while Speaker Mike Johnson, who gets an outsize four votes in Steering matters, said he would leave the waiver debate to the panel.

"We haven't gotten to that yet," Johnson told POLITICO. "We'll figure it out."

There is some precedent for granting waivers.

In 2022, North Carolina Rep. Virginia Foxx , then the chair of the Education and Workforce Committee, successfully applied for a waiver after Republicans retook the majority after four years of Democratic control. She argued she'd had only two years as chair and had more work to get done .

Two years later, Transportation and Infrastructure Chair Sam Graves of Missouri made his pitch to stay for a fourth term, and was granted a waiver to the surprise of several Republicans.

One key factor: Both Foxx and Graves had backing from members of their committees, including those next in line for the position. That doesn't appear to be the case this time around.

Now, not only is Scott looking to immediately succeed Thompson, but Rogers is facing challenges from Reps. Ronny Jackson of Texas, Rob Wittman of Virginia and Trent Kelly of Mississippi. Westerman hasn't officially thrown his hat into the ring, but Rep. Pete Stauber of Minnesota is already in the Natural Resources race , and Rep. Paul Gosar of Arizona has floated interest.

"I support term limits. I always have. It wouldn't matter if I was in this race or not," Scott said. "There are some other people that are very good friends of mine that are termed out, and I would not support a term limit for them."

Rogers hasn't disclosed his specific pitch for a waiver, saying in an interview at the Capitol earlier this month that he's "not going to talk about that before the election."

Thompson, meanwhile, has already circulated a letter to Steering Committee members asking for their support, citing his "temperament and willingness to roll up my sleeves to get the job done." Notably, it remains uncertain whether Congress will be able to pass a farm bill this year — typically a crowning achievement for any Agriculture chair.

Matt Brennan, Thompson's chief of staff, said in a statement that the chair is focused on the November election but "will continue to make his intentions known to members of the Steering Committee and the conference at large in the coming weeks."

Some Republicans believe the issue could solve itself, especially if the GOP loses its majority in November and the chairs would instead be looking at two years as ranking members. And others simply believe the number of lawmakers seeking exceptions will work against all of them. The last time multiple chairs sought waivers, in 2010, both were denied.

"The more people that apply for waivers, the less likely any of them are to happen because then you're in a position of having to make choices," Cole said. "Either they all get it or they all don't get it."

Connor O'Brien and Grace Yarrow contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump administration turns to Supreme Court as third-country deportations are thrown into question
articles.summary: A ruling to halt deportations of people to countries other than their own threw a core immigration policy of the Trump administration into question, at least...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A ruling to halt deportations of people to countries other than their own threw a core immigration policy of the Trump administration into question, at least temporarily, and prompted a desperate appeal to the Supreme Court on Thursday.

The administration said the ruling by the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals came Wednesday just minutes before midnight, forcing the cancellation of a flight with 70 people that was headed to three countries. It said justices needed to step in to "halt that chaos" and said the flight cancellation "required a new round of diplomatic engagement with each of the three countries," which it did not name.

Plaintiffs for immigrants sought emergency relief from the appeals court Wednesday night, saying they heard from "multiple sources" that a deportation flight was scheduled the next day from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Burundi, Rwanda and the Central African Republic.

Within hours of that request, the appeals court said it was clarifying a ruling against the policy last week and said a previous order allowing flights to continue while legal challenges play out was no longer in effect.

Administration officials reacted furiously. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the order "in the dark of night" robbed authorities of "an entirely legal and valuable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration."

The justices previously allowed the deportation flights to temporarily continue when the case came before them last year.

The vast majority of people deported to countries other than their own have been sent to Mexico, but under a series of often-secret agreements, the administration has deported thousands of others to more than two dozen countries, from Liberia to Guyana.

Some have found themselves in countries they'd never heard of before their arrivals and held there against their will. Some also face serious safety risks, and are left with little choice except to return to the home countries they were fleeing.

This month, lawyers for two men deported to Equatorial Guinea said they were beaten and held at gunpoint in a hotel-turned-detention center by police who covered their heads with bags.

Trump's Republican administration has said that it sends people with final deportation orders to third countries when their homelands won't accept them or they can't be returned there. Those governments provide assurances that people won't be persecuted or tortured, attorneys said.

James Percival, the Department of Homeland Security's general counsel, said Wednesday on X that 25,000 people in the U.S. illegally have been deported to third countries, calling those deportations "an essential public safety tool."

The lower court order doesn't completely prohibit third-country deportations, but it requires the government give people a meaningful chance to object .

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to halt that decision, arguing it would force unreasonable delays and the reworking of agreements with foreign countries.

"The order below would again obstruct DHS from efficiently removing aliens ... by inordinately delaying third-country removal for any alien who voices a fear of persecution or torture in that country, no matter how frivolous or belated the claim," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.

The appeal comes amid a sweeping immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, which has pledged to deport millions of people who are living in the United States illegally.

Tim Sullivan contributed to this report from Minneapolis. Follow the AP's coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at .

articles.title: We aren’t trying to kill Trump, Iran’s president insists to reporters at New York hotel
articles.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian sat down to face questions from a group of journalists in New York on Thursday amid the war with the US.
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's media appearances in Iran are tightly controlled affairs.

But on Thursday he sat down to face questions from a group of journalists in New York, where despite being the leader of a country at war with the United States, he is visiting with the protection of the US Secret Service.

In the wide-ranging session, a day after addressing the UN General Assembly, Pezeshkian repeated familiar Iranian positions on the war, its nuclear program and dissent in Iran. He also talked about the effect of sanctions on the Iranian people, and claimed Iran would never try to kill Donald Trump – despite the president and US authorities accusing the regime of plotting his assassination.

The comments were made at the Millennium Hilton hotel, a stone's throw from the UN headquarters where the Iranian president declared Wednesday that his country "will not bow down" as the war with the US drags on.

In the briefing, Pezeshkian also described recent meetings he had held with Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since the outset of the war, saying that the leader was "quite healthy."

There has been mounting speculation in recent months over Khamenei's health, after he was understood to have sustained serious injuries in the US-Israeli attack that killed his father and predecessor Ali Khamenei at the beginning of the conflict in February.

Speaking about Khamenei's condition, Pezeshkian said, "I did not see any major challenges with his health or physical appearance," adding that their most recent in-person meeting had taken place around one month ago and lasted around seven hours.

Pezeshkian said the pair had sat on pillows on the ground and stood up to walk around during the meeting. US intelligence assesses that despite his injuries Khamenei is still playing a critical role in shaping war strategy alongside senior Iranian officials, multiple sources familiar with the intelligence said in May.

The presence of Iran's delegation in a country with which it remains at war is already virtually unprecedented.

But this spectacle became increasingly unconventional on Thursday when the Iranian president and Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi briefed reporters including from CNN in a hotel function room in Midtown Manhattan.

A State Department official said earlier this week that the visiting Iranian delegates were "being admitted to the United States strictly for the purpose of representing the Islamic Republic of Iran before the United Nations" and that they must "restrict their activities to United Nations-related business only."

The Iranians "must seek and receive approval in advance" from the State Department if they want to travel outside the vicinity of the UN headquarters, John F. Kennedy International Airport or Iran's UN mission facilities, the official said.

In the briefing, Pezeshkian denied accusations that Iran was trying to kill the president, saying it has "never been the position [of the Iranian government], overtly or covertly, to seek to assassinate Trump or his family members."

Last month, the US Secret Service said it was aware of a video aired by Iran's state broadcaster appearing to threaten the life of Barron Trump , the president's youngest son. This came after Israel shared intelligence with the US that Iran had devised a plan to assassinate Donald Trump. In late 2024, the US Justice Department announced federal charges over what it described as a thwarted Iranian plot to kill Trump before the presidential election.

Hard-line Iranian media have repeatedly featured content threatening the life of Trump and his family. During funeral events for the late Khamenei in July, regime loyalists were seen holding posters with the words "Kill Trump." Trump has publicly discussed the Iranian threats on his life too, saying in July: "I'm on whatever list … so far, I guess I've been a bit lucky, but maybe that doesn't last very long. These are evil, sick people."

In response to Pezeshkian's comments, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said, "The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region."

"The president is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable," Kelly said.

Pezeshkian also discussed the domestic challenges facing Iran. US sanctions and the ongoing war have suffocated the country's economy , sparking prices increases and shortages of basic necessities.

The Iranian president also said in the session that Iran wants a deal, but that any agreement was not related to the timing of the US midterms.

Separately, also on Thursday, Araghchi said Iran had presented a proposal to the US that — according to Iran — would re-open the Strait of Hormuz and restart negotiations toward a "final deal."

The proposal, presented to the US through mediators this week, calls for the US to meet certain conditions within seven days to restart the talks and re-open the strait, Araghchi said. The foreign minister declined to elaborate on the conditions but said that they were "nothing more" than what was included in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.

That agreement, which was reached by the two countries in June, included provisions on sanctions relief; the release of frozen assets; and a cessation of military operations, including in Lebanon.

In response to Araghchi's comments, a White House official told CNN they were having "positive and constructive discussions through the mediators."

Iran's economy was in a dire state even before the war began, with the poor conditions a key driving factor behind the anti-regime demonstrations which kicked off in the Iranian capital city Tehran in 2025.

"We have problems. Unprecedentedly difficult problems," Pezeshkian told reporters Thursday, while referring to US sanctions as a "silent murderous campaign."

Much like in his Wednesday address to world leaders, Pezeshkian appeared confident in the briefing that Iran would prevail despite the challenges facing his country. He also insisted that US bases in the region were legitimate targets as they had been used to attack Iran.

"Most of the American bases in the region are no longer useable," he claimed.

Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases across the Middle East region during the war's first months, according to an official Pentagon watchdog report released earlier this month.

"Of course, the US has the power to destroy anything anywhere, but it is impossible to bring about Iranian surrender," Pezeshkian said.

CNN's Jennifer Hansler, Holmes Lybrand, Todd Symons, Zachary Cohen, Natasha Bertrand and Jim Sciutto contributed reporting.

articles.summary: A nova pesquisa Quaest para o Senado no RN mostra Styvenson Valentim na liderança e aponta que 61% dos eleitores seguem indecisos na consulta espontânea.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta sexta-feira (25) mostra como está a disputa pelo Senado eno Rio Grande do Norte. O levantamento foi encomendado pela Inter TV.

Em 2026, serão eleitos dois senadores em cada estado e no Distrito Federal, para renovar 54 das 81 cadeiras. Por isso, cada eleitor precisa votar em dois candidatos diferentes. Não é possível escolher o mesmo nome duas vezes.

Na pesquisa espontânea da Quaest — em que os nomes não são mostrados aos eleitores entrevistados —, 61% estão indecisos, porque não souberam citar um candidato.

Já na pesquisa estimulada, a lista de candidatos é mostrada, e cada entrevistado precisa responder duas vezes em quem pretende votar: para a primeira vaga e, depois, para a segunda vaga.

Os resultados da pesquisa para o Senado consideram as menções para a primeira e a segunda vagas em um total que soma 100% das intenções de voto e mantém a proporção entre candidatos, brancos/nulos e indecisos. Veja os números abaixo:

articles.body:
Debate do g1 com candidatos ao Senado de São Paulo — Foto: Noah Denser/Divulgação

O g1 promoveu, nesta sexta-feira (25), uma rodada de debate com candidatos ao Senado por São Paulo . O encontro foi realizado às 13h e reuniu quatro candidatos às duas vagas, com mediação da jornalista Ana Paula Campos.

Assista, na íntegra, aos debates abaixo e, mais adiante na reportagem, confira blocos temáticos de respostas e as considerações finais.

Participaram do debate Geraldo Rufino (Podemos), Marina Silva (Rede), Simone Tebet (PSB) e Soninha Francine (Cidadania). André do Prado (PL) e Guilherme Derrite (PP) haviam confirmado presença, mas anunciaram horas antes que não iriam participar.

Conforme as regras estabelecidas, foram convidados os candidatos de partidos e federações com representação mínima de cinco parlamentares no Congresso Nacional. Também seriam chamados outros candidatos que alcançassem pelo menos 5% de intenções de voto na pesquisa mais recente, a Datafolha divulgada no dia 11, mas nenhum deles atingiu essa pontuação.

Ao longo das duas rodadas, os candidatos discutiram temas como meio ambiente; emendas parlamentares; crime organizado; trabalho e emprego, educação e relação entre poderes. No fim, ainda tiveram tempo para as considerações finais.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro chama proibição das bets de 'estelionato eleitoral' | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PL à Presidência criticou adversário por anunciar medida provisória a nove dias do 1º turno das eleições.
articles.summary: Por meio de Medida Provisória, Lula anunciou nesta sexta (25) a proibição total de apostas online. Vedação inclui jogos online e cassinos virtuais, como o "Jogo do Tigrinho".
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro durante live na noite de 23 de setembro — Foto: Reprodução

O candidato do PL à Presidência da República, Flávio Bolsonaro, criticou Lula (PT) pela decisão de proibir, a nove dias da eleição, a operação das empresas de apostas esportivas (bets) no Brasil.

Em um vídeo de campanha postado nas redes sociais, Flávio disse que Lula age de forma oportunista e chamou a Medida Provisória (MP) anunciada nesta sexta-feira (25) de "estelionato eleitoral" e "solução fajuta".

"Faz por medida provisória, que tem duração só de quatro meses. Depois das eleições, se a MP caducar, as bets podem voltar com força total. Mas aí já vai ser tarde, porque as eleições já vão ter passado e ele já enganou milhões de eleitores", disse Flávio Bolsonaro.

O candidato do PL disse que, se for eleito, não vai permitir durante seu mandato "cassino online, nem Tigrinho". Ele não menciona as bets.

Por meio de Medida Provisória, Lula anunciou nesta sexta a proibição total de apostas online . A vedação inclui jogos online e cassinos virtuais, como o "Jogo do Tigrinho".

🔎 As MPs são publicadas pelo governo federal e passam a valer com força de lei imediatamente, mas devem ser votadas pelo Congresso em até 120 dias. Se isso não acontecer, perdem a validade.

Lula também enviou ao Congresso um projeto de lei que estabelece penas de prisão para quem explorar, operar ou divulgar as chamadas bets. Nesse caso, a medida precisa passar por votação de deputados e senadores para começar a valer.

Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou que Lula usou a arrecadação de impostos pagos pelas empresas de apostas para "cobrir rombos do governo" e agora faz "politicagem" com o tema.

"Ele deveria ter combatido as bets desde o início. Desde que o Lula regulamentou as bets, o governo já arrecadou mais de R$ 20 bilhões", disse. "Se estivesse minimamente preocupado, não tinha autorizado as bets a funcionarem dois anos atrás", afirmou.

A legislação aprovada naquela época previa que o governo deveria criar regras para o setor em até dois anos, prazo que poderia ser prorrogado por mais dois anos — ou seja, até o fim de 2022, o que não ocorreu. Esse período coincide com o governo de Jair Bolsonaro, pai de Flávio.

A aprovação ocorreu somente em 2023, já no governo Lula. A norma estabeleceu regras para a operação das bets, definiu os impostos a serem pagos por empresas e apostadores e como o governo poderia gastar o dinheiro arrecadado com essa atividade.

Originalmente, o governo enviou ao Congresso uma proposa com regras para empresas de apostas sobre eventos esportivos, como partidas de futebol.

Durante as discussões na Câmara, o texto foi alterado para incluir também os jogos online, como os cassinos virtuais. Essa versão acabou aprovada e virou lei no fim de 2023.

articles.title: Mulher denuncia o pai após filha relatar que foi estuprada pelo avô | G1
articles.standfirst: Adolescente relatou ter sofrido abusos na casa do avô desde os 8 anos. A mãe afirma que, na infância, também sofreu abusos dentro de casa.
articles.summary: Adolescente relatou ter sofrido abusos na casa do avô desde os 8 anos. A mãe afirma que, na infância, também sofreu abusos dentro de casa.
articles.body:
Mulher denuncia o pai após filha relatar que era estuprada pelo avô, em Fortaleza — Foto: Divulgação/EBC

Um homem de 51 anos foi denunciado à polícia por suspeita de cometer estupro de vulnerável contra a própria neta, de 12 anos, em Fortaleza . A mãe da vítima ouviu o relato e registrou boletim de ocorrência contra o próprio pai. Ela afirma que, na infância, também sofreu abusos dentro de casa .

A denúncia pelo crime de estupro de vulnerável , ocorrida no bairro Parque Presidente Vargas, é investigada pela Delegacia de Combate à Exploração da Criança e do Adolescente (Dececa). O inquérito policial foi instaurado nesta sexta-feira (25).

Em nota, a defesa do suspeito afirmou que acompanha a situação e que ele está à disposição das autoridades para prestar esclarecimentos (veja mais abaixo) . A reportagem não divulga o nome da mãe e do avô para preservar a identidade da criança.

Ao g1 , a mulher contou que descobriu a situação quando a filha de 12 anos resolveu contar para ela que já tinha sido estuprada pelo avô. O relato foi feito pela adolescente, que chegou da escola abalada depois de ter ouvido comentários sobre abusos sexuais .

A garota falou para a mãe que percebeu, aos 8 anos de idade, que o avô olhava para ela de forma diferente e que, inicialmente, ele passava a mão nas partes íntimas dela. E relatou que, depois de um tempo, passou a ser estuprada por ele.

A adolescente também contou que o último estupro foi cometido há cerca de 2 meses, quando o homem teria também ignorado reclamações dela ao sentir dores durante o abuso.

“Eu já fiquei muito nervosa e acreditei de imediato, justamente por conta das coisas que já tinham acontecido comigo porque, quando eu era criança, ele também tinha me abusado… Só que, como eu era muito criança, eu nem entendia o que tinha acontecido comigo”, contou a mãe.

A mãe levou a adolescente à delegacia, onde a denúncia foi formalizada com um boletim de ocorrência. Em seguida, a menina passou por exames e procedimentos de prevenção das Infecções Sexualmente Transmissíveis (ISTs).

Apesar de relatar ter sofrido abusos na infância, a mãe da adolescente conta que nunca havia denunciado o pai e tinha resolvido esquecer o que havia passado. Ela detalhou que, na vida adulta, passou a confiar na dedicação que o pai demonstrava ao acompanhar as netas desde o nascimento.

“ Eu fico me responsabilizando o tempo todo, me culpando, me sentindo a pior das mães . Porque eu deixei isso acontecer com ela. Na minha cabeça, eu poderia ter impedido. E, infelizmente, eu não consegui, mas eu vou até onde eu tiver que ir agora pra que a justiça seja feita por ela”, contou a mãe.

Depois de fazer a denúncia, ela afirmou que a filha deve passar por acompanhamento psicológico . “Ela fala pra mim que só quer que isso acabe logo, que ela quer voltar a viver a vida dela normalmente”, explicou.

O contato do suspeito com a adolescente era frequente. Ela e a irmã mais nova passavam fins de semana na casa dele. Conforme a mãe, alguns episódios fizeram com que ela deixasse de enviar as filhas para ficar com o avô. Um deles foi o pedido da filha mais velha de não ir mais até lá.

“Ela não estava querendo muito ir para a casa dele. E isso até me estranhou porque ela sempre ficava muito animada de ir para a casa dele por conta dos passeios, dos brinquedos, dos presentes, do que o mesmo fazia por elas”, conta a mãe.

Segundo ela, a adolescente contou que os abusos aconteciam quando ele estava em casa sem a esposa dele . A atual companheira do suspeito não é avó das crianças.

Há cerca de 2 meses, a mãe das meninas recebeu da esposa dele mensagens informando que ela havia encontrado conteúdos de pornografia infantil no celular dele. Segundo a mãe, a companheira dele também contou ter visto conversas dele com crianças e adolescentes.

A partir destas informações, ela declara que ficou bastante assustada e que preferiu interromper o contato das filhas com ele. Desde então, ela não deixou mais que ele visse as netas.

Em nota, o advogado Victor Fernandes Tavares informou que a defesa do suspeito “tem conhecimento da acusação mencionada pela reportagem e acompanha a situação com a seriedade que ela exige ”.

A defesa mencionou também que, até o momento, não foi informada da instauração do procedimento formal e que o suspeito está à disposição das autoridades competentes para prestar esclarecimentos, caso seja chamado.

“Em respeito à delicadeza da situação e às pessoas envolvidas, a defesa não comentará publicamente os detalhes da acusação. Reitera a importância de uma apuração responsável, com observância do devido processo legal e da presunção de inocência”, conclui a nota.

articles.title: TikTok firma acordo de até R$ 1,5 bilhão e terá de impor limite de 2 horas por dia | G1
articles.standfirst: Acordo prevê limite de duas horas de uso por dia, pausas após 15 minutos e medidas mais rígidas para verificar a idade dos usuários; estado acusava plataforma de contribuir para problemas de saúde mental entre adolescentes.
articles.summary: Acordo prevê limite de duas horas de uso por dia, pausas após 15 minutos e medidas mais rígidas para verificar a idade dos usuários; estado acusava plataforma de contribuir para pr
articles.body:
O TikTok e sua controladora chinesa, a ByteDance, chegaram a um acordo com o estado do Alabama nesta sexta-feira (25), dias antes do início de um julgamento sobre acusações de que a plataforma é viciante e enganou consumidores sobre sua segurança.

O estado receberá pelo menos US$ 100 milhões (R$ 510 milhões) em até 45 dias, e o valor poderá chegar a US$ 300 milhões (R$ 1.53 bilhão) caso determinadas condições sejam cumpridas , segundo o gabinete do procurador-geral do Alabama, procurado pela Reuters.

Como parte do acordo, o TikTok também terá de fazer mudanças na plataforma.

Uum limite de duas horas de uso por dia;

Mecanismos mais rigorosos para verificar a idade dos usuários.

É o primeiro acordo do TikTok com um estado americano em meio a uma série de processos semelhantes. Ao menos outros 27 estados e Washington, D.C., também processaram a empresa por questões relacionadas aos efeitos da plataforma sobre crianças e adolescentes.

O julgamento estava previsto para começar na segunda-feira (28), em um tribunal estadual de Montgomery, capital do Alabama, e deveria durar de duas a três semanas.

O processo poderia oferecer uma rara visão sobre o funcionamento interno do TikTok, que já chegou a acordos em outros casos que haviam sido selecionados para julgamento e vinha tentando manter em sigilo informações sobre a operação da plataforma.

Algoritmo direciona jovens para vídeos de violência

O processo do Alabama foi apresentado no ano passado pelo procurador-geral do estado, Steve Marshall, do Partido Republicano. O estado havia acusado o TikTok de usar um fluxo contínuo de vídeos, que nunca termina, para tornar a plataforma altamente viciante.

Segundo a ação, o algoritmo — sistema que seleciona e recomenda conteúdos para cada usuário — direciona jovens para vídeos cada vez mais intensos sobre violência e automutilação.

O Alabama afirmou que isso contribuiu para uma crise de saúde mental entre adolescentes e fez o número de atendimentos de emergência por casos de automutilação no estado “disparar”.

O estado também acusou o TikTok de afirmar falsamente que restringe o acesso de jovens a conteúdos sexuais e violentos para conseguir uma classificação que indique que o aplicativo é seguro para adolescentes nas lojas de aplicativos do Google, da Apple e da Microsoft.

Outra acusação era a de que a empresa teria enganado usuários sobre o acesso do governo chinês aos dados de americanos.

O TikTok afirma que desenvolveu sua plataforma tendo a segurança de adolescentes como uma de suas principais prioridades.

A empresa também argumentou que a Seção 230 da Lei Federal de Decência nas Comunicações, uma regra americana que limita a responsabilidade das plataformas por conteúdos publicados pelos próprios usuários, a protege de processos relacionados a esse tipo de conteúdo.

Representantes do TikTok não responderam imediatamente a um pedido de comentário da Reuters.

Multa de mais de R$ 150 milhões: ANPD afirma que TikTok falhou na proteção de informações de crianças e adolescentes — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

articles.title: Estudo do NetLab indica que Kwai descumpre regras do TSE sobre anúncios eleitorais | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisadores apontam falta de detalhamento sobre gastos e alcance e ausência de dados sobre a audiência. Plataforma diz que suas ferramentas atendem a regulamentações do TSE.
articles.summary: Estudo da UFRJ aponta falta de precisão sobre gastos e alcance, ausência de dados sobre a audiência e limitações de acesso aos anúncios.
articles.body:
Prédio do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral é visto durante o entardecer em Brasília — Foto: Antonio Augusto/Secom/TSE

Um estudo do NetLab, laboratório da Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), aponta que o Kwai não cumpre integralmente as exigências do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) para publicidade político-eleitoral e dificulta a fiscalização dos anúncios pagos que circulam na plataforma. O material foi obtido com exclusividade pelo g1 .

O levantamento não demonstra que anúncios irregulares estejam circulando no Kwai. O problema apontado é a falta de condições para verificar de maneira abrangente se isso ocorre. Segundo o NetLab, essa mesma análise será feita em outras plataformas que oferecem anúncios, como TikTok e Meta (Instagram e Facebook).

Segundo o documento sobre o Kwai, a biblioteca de anúncios da rede social não informa com precisão os gastos e a quantidade de pessoas atingidas, não apresenta o perfil do público efetivamente alcançado e limita a busca e a coleta de dados. A NetLab disse que vai apresentar o levantamento ao TSE.

O detalhamento de informações e ferramentas é exigido pela Justiça Eleitoral. A regulamentação estabelece que o cumprimento das obrigações de transparência é requisito para o credenciamento de empresas que pretendam oferecer impulsionamento eleitoral, serviço pago por campanhas para ampliar a distribuição de conteúdos.

Em resposta ao g1 , o Kwai afirmou que seu Plano de Conformidade Eleitoral para 2026 foi revisado e aprovado pelo TSE e que suas ferramentas foram desenvolvidas para atender à regulamentação. A empresa disse que o acesso à ferramenta que permite extrair dados automaticamente para analisar anúncios em escala é possível mediante solicitação pelo Portal de Solicitação de Aplicação da Lei.

“Eventuais falhas técnicas identificadas em seu funcionamento serão analisadas pelas equipes responsáveis, com a adoção dos ajustes necessários, quando aplicável”, informou o Kwai.

Procurado, o TSE informou que o conteúdo do relatório está sendo avaliado e que "tomará providências" nos termos da resolução que trata da propaganda eleitoral.

Em entrevista ao g1 , a diretora do NetLab, Marie Santini, explicou que as limitações impedem verificar se há publicidade irregular circulando na plataforma.

“O TSE tem que proibir o Kwai de rodar anúncios, porque ele não está atendendo às resoluções. E isso pode estar interferindo na eleição. É uma plataforma que tem uma audiência muito grande na rede brasileira: 40% dos usuários brasileiros usam o Kwai, só que é mais classe C, D e E, não é classe A e B. [...] Tem mais usuários que o LinkedIn e o X e está rodando anúncio sem cumprir a resolução. Então, é um ambiente propício para ter muito anúncio irregular, campanha irregular, e a gente não está conseguindo observar”, afirmou.

O Kwai participou, em 16 de julho, de uma reunião entre o presidente do TSE, ministro Nunes Marques, e representantes de plataformas digitais para firmar compromissos de combate à desinformação nas eleições.

A empresa mantém ainda uma colaboração com o tribunal para disponibilizar orientações oficiais sobre o pleito de 2026 dentro da plataforma.

Presidente do TSE, ministro Nunes Marques, em reunião com representantes de plataformas digitais para firmar parcerias contra a desinformação, em 16 de julho de 2026 — Foto: Luiz Roberto/TSE

Os pesquisadores do NetLab avaliaram a Biblioteca de Anúncios Políticos ou Eleitorais do Kwai a partir de 11 critérios baseados nas normas do tribunal. Segundo o estudo, cinco não foram atendidos, três foram cumpridos integralmente e três tiveram atendimento parcial ou não puderam ser plenamente verificados.

A equipe analisou ainda funcionalidades de busca, consulta, filtragem e extração de dados. O levantamento foi encerrado em 16 de setembro de 2026.

Gastos : divulgação de faixas de valores, sem informar quanto foi efetivamente desembolsado por anúncio.

Alcance : apresentação de intervalos amplos de exibições, sem precisão sobre a quantidade de pessoas atingidas.

Audiência : ausência das características do público que efetivamente recebeu a publicidade.

Busca : impossibilidade de pesquisar anúncios por palavras-chave ou termos de interesse.

Coleta : ausência de uma API, ferramenta que permite extrair dados automaticamente para analisar anúncios em escala.

Biblioteca de anúncios do Kwai apresenta gastos de campanhas em faixas de valores e campo de busca pelo nome do anunciante — Foto: Reprodução

🔎 Uma API é um recurso que permite que sites, aplicativos e outros sistemas troquem dados e acionem funcionalidades entre si, seguindo regras predefinidas. Por exemplo, é por meio de uma API que um aplicativo no seu celular consegue acessar e atualizar dados da previsão do tempo fornecidos pelos sistemas de empresas de meteorologia.

Busca limitada dificulta identificar publicidade irregular

O artigo 27-A da Resolução nº 23.610/2019, introduzido pela Resolução nº 23.732/2024, determina que as plataformas ofereçam buscas por palavras-chave, termos de interesse e nomes de anunciantes. No Kwai, segundo o estudo, só a última opção está disponível.

A diferença tem consequência direta para a fiscalização: para encontrar um anúncio, o pesquisador precisa conhecer previamente quem pagou por ele. Isso dificulta localizar publicidade contratada por pessoas ou páginas que não estejam autorizadas a realizar impulsionamento eleitoral.

“Quando você coloca que tem que buscar pelo anunciante, isso me obriga a saber de antemão qual é o anunciante problemático”, disse Santini.

Uma busca pelo conteúdo permitiria localizar, por exemplo, anúncios que mencionassem “urna eletrônica” ou trouxessem um pedido de voto, independentemente de quem os contratou. Sem esse recurso, é necessário percorrer as peças de cada anunciante conhecido.

“Para a gente saber se está rodando anúncio irregular ou ilegal, a gente tem que conseguir buscar, percorrer os anúncios independentemente dos anunciantes”, explicou.

A própria resolução estabelece que um conteúdo pode ser considerado político-eleitoral independentemente da classificação feita pela plataforma. A definição abrange temas como eleições, candidatos, partidos, propostas de governo e exercício do direito ao voto.

Segundo o NetLab, porém, a biblioteca torna visíveis apenas os anúncios que o Kwai classifica como político-eleitorais. Isso limita a possibilidade de verificar se peças que deveriam estar nessa categoria ficaram de fora.

Essa fiscalização também depende da possibilidade de reunir e analisar grandes volumes de dados. Por isso, o mesmo artigo da resolução exige uma API, que é uma interface que permite coletar automaticamente informações sobre conteúdo, gastos, alcance, público atingido e responsáveis pelo pagamento.

Segundo o estudo, o Kwai não oferece essa ferramenta. Santini explica que, sem ela, os pesquisadores precisam recorrer à coleta manual ou à raspagem de dados na interface da plataforma, métodos que dificultam garantir que todos os anúncios e suas informações foram obtidos.

“Com a API não só você consegue aprofundar e ter vários detalhes e metadados, como você consegue fazer uma coleta sistemática”, afirmou.

Além de permitir localizar e coletar os anúncios, a regulamentação exige informações precisas sobre o dinheiro gasto e a quantidade de pessoas atingidas. Segundo o estudo, o Kwai apresenta esses dados em faixas amplas.

Para despesas de até R$ 5 mil por anúncio, os intervalos são de R$ 500, como de R$ 0 a R$ 500 e de R$ 500 a R$ 1 mil. Acima desse patamar, as faixas podem chegar a R$ 1 mil ou R$ 5 mil.

Assim, uma peça que custou R$ 10 e outra que custou R$ 500 podem aparecer na mesma categoria. Na avaliação de Santini, isso dificulta auditar os gastos das campanhas e comparar os valores cobrados dos anunciantes.

“Uma das coisas que o TSE exigiu fosse que o valor do anúncio seja colocado, exatamente o valor que foi pago”, disse.

A imprecisão se repete nos dados de circulação. A maioria dos anúncios verificados entre 26 de agosto e 16 de setembro aparecia com a indicação de “menos de 5 milhões de impressões”. Também foram encontradas faixas de 5 milhões a 10 milhões e de 10 milhões a 30 milhões.

Um anúncio exibido 100 vezes e outro exibido 4,5 milhões de vezes, portanto, poderiam receber a mesma indicação.

🔎 Impressões são exibições de um anúncio, que pode aparecer mais de uma vez para a mesma pessoa. A exigência do TSE é informar com precisão a quantidade de pessoas atingidas.

A norma também determina a divulgação das características dos grupos que compõem a audiência da publicidade. Nesse caso, o estudo distingue o público que o anunciante pretende alcançar daquele que efetivamente recebe a mensagem.

A biblioteca do Kwai mostra critérios escolhidos para direcionar os anúncios, como idade, gênero, região, marca do celular e sistema operacional. Mas, segundo o NetLab, não apresenta o perfil do público efetivamente atingido.

Também faltam informações sobre o direcionamento por interesses. Embora a plataforma ofereça essa possibilidade aos anunciantes, os pesquisadores não encontraram dados sobre seu uso nas peças examinadas.

Para Santini, essas lacunas dificultam verificar como os dados dos usuários são usados para distribuir propaganda política e se os limites legais são respeitados.

A resolução prevê proteção contra discriminação ilícita e abusiva e exige, como regra, consentimento específico, expresso e destacado para o tratamento de dados pessoais sensíveis na propaganda eleitoral. A falta de informações na biblioteca não comprova uso irregular desses dados, mas restringe sua fiscalização.

Na avaliação de Santini, os problemas mostram que a existência de uma biblioteca pública não basta para assegurar transparência.

“Ou seja, ela é a transparência de fachada”, afirmou, ao criticar a dificuldade de localizar publicidade de anunciantes desconhecidos.

A pesquisadora defende que o Kwai deixe de veicular anúncios políticos até adequar suas ferramentas.

A resolução do TSE estabelece que as exigências de transparência são permanentes, inclusive fora do período eleitoral. Para empresas que passaram a oferecer impulsionamento após a entrada em vigor da regra, as medidas devem estar disponíveis desde o início da prestação do serviço.

Na Política Eleitoral do Kwai, identificada como atualizada em junho de 2026, a plataforma afirma trabalhar em colaboração com autoridades locais para garantir a integridade das eleições.

O documento permite a contratação de anúncios politicamente relevantes, desde que estejam de acordo com a legislação eleitoral e com as políticas da plataforma. Prevê identificação de conteúdo patrocinado, rotulagem do uso de inteligência artificial e inclusão do anúncio e do anunciante na biblioteca pública.

A política também prevê a remoção de alegações de fraude sem evidências verificáveis e proíbe conteúdos políticos enganosos produzidos ou manipulados por inteligência artificial, incluindo deepfakes .

🔎 Deepfake é uma técnica que permite alterar um vídeo ou foto com ajuda de inteligência artificial (IA). Com ele, por exemplo, o rosto da pessoa que está em cena pode ser trocado pelo de outra; ou aquilo que a pessoa fala pode ser modificado.

O estudo aponta que os compromissos declarados não se traduzem integralmente nos mecanismos de transparência oferecidos pelo Kwai para fiscalizar a publicidade.

articles.title: Brasil e EUA se reúnem na OMC para discutir tarifaço; prazo para acordo é de 60 dias | G1
articles.standfirst: Brasil apresentou pedido de consultas à OMC, e Estados Unidos se disseram ‘à disposição’ para conversar, mas ainda não há sinais de reversão. Se ao final dos 60 dias não houver um acordo, os países podem pedir a abertura de um painel.
articles.summary: Brasil apresentou pedido de consultas à OMC, e Estados Unidos se disseram ‘à disposição’ para conversar, mas ainda não há sinais de reversão. Se ao final dos 60 dias não houver um acordo, os países podem pedir a abertura de um painel.
articles.body:
Representantes dos presidentes Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Donald Trump se reuniram nesta sexta-feira (25) na sede da Organização Mundial do Comércio ( OMC ), em Genebra (Suíça), para discutir o processo aberto pelo Brasil para questionar as tarifas impostas pelo governo dos Estados Unidos a produtos brasileiros vendidos no mercado americano.

A informação foi confirmada pelo Ministério das Relações Exteriores .

Na prática, a partir dessa primeira rodada de negociação, passa a valer o prazo de 60 dias para que os dois países cheguem a um consenso sobre as tarifas.

Se ao final desse prazo não houver um acordo, qualquer um dos dois pode pedir a abertura de um painel, ou seja, o julgamento em si do tema pela OMC.

Do lado do Brasil, participaram os secretários do Ministério das Relações Exteriores Philip Fox Gough (Assuntos Econômicos) e Maurício Lyrio (Clima e Meio Ambiente), entre outras autoridades.

Conforme o Itamaraty, nāo houve decisão.

O pedido de consultas foi apresentado em julho deste ano . No documento, o Brasil questionou os dois tarifaços:

de 25%: diante do entendimento da Casa Branca de práticas desleais do Brasil em relação a empresários americanos em áreas como PIX, desmatamento e propriedade intelectual;

de 12,5%: em razão do entendimento dos EUA de que dezenas de países, incluindo o Brasil, falharam ao coibir a importação de mercadorias produzidas onde há trabalho forçado.

No pedido à OMC, formalizado em 30 de julho, o Brasil afirma que, ao agir dessa maneira, os EUA tratam o país de maneira diferente dos demais parceiros comerciais e ferem compromissos firmados junto à entidade.

Na resposta ao pedido de consultas, enviada em 10 de agosto, os EUA aceitaram o pedido e se disseram “à disposição” para discutir o tema .

Segundo integrantes do governo brasileiro, ainda não há, contudo, indicativo de reversão do tarifaço a partir do processo na OMC.

No mesmo dia em que os EUA aceitaram o pedido de consultas, o governo da China pediu formalmente para participar o processo na OMC.

Nesta semana, porém, os EUA responderam afirmando serem contra a presença dos chineses nas conversas.

Sem acordo com Brasil, EUA impuseram tarifas de 25% contra alguns produtos — Foto: Joao Oliveira/Zoonar/picture alliance

Ao longo de todo o processo de negociação entre os dois países, integrantes do governo brasileiro disseram avaliar que a motivação do tarifaço contra produtores brasileiros era política e não comercial.

Os negociadores brasileiros citam entre os pontos que levaram a essa conclusão, por exemplo:

os EUA alegarem que têm déficit comercial com o Brasil , quando, na verdade, a relação é superavitária para os americanos;

os EUA argumentarem que o Brasil não combate o desmatamento como deveria, uma vez que os dados dos últimos anos mostram queda no desmatamento ilegal;

os EUA afirmarem que o Brasil falha ao importar mercadoria onde há trabalho forçado enquanto a OIT reconhece o país como referência no combate ao trabalho forçado.

Integrantes do governo Lula dizem, ainda, ver o tarifaço americano como uma forma de tentar pressionar o governo em ano eleitoral. O objetivo seria prejudicar o petista e ajudar o candidato do PL, Flávio Bolsonaro, com quem Trump se reuniu em Washington em maio deste ano .

Segundo auxiliares de Lula que participaram da recente conversa telefônica entre ele e Trump, o presidente americano deu sinais de que não tem conhecimento dos pormenores do tarifaço.

Esse cenário indicou para o governo brasileiro que a decisão partiu de Jamieson Greer, representante comercial da Casa Branca, e de integrantes do Departamento de Estado, onde tem havido a prevalência da ala mais ideológica do governo sobre os diplomatas profissionais.

articles.title: Trump’s odd midterm strategy: Give voters the opposite of what they want
articles.summary: There’s a simple way to understand Republicans’ apparent plight ahead of the midterm elections.
articles.body:
There's a simple way to understand Republicans' apparent plight ahead of the midterm elections.

New CNN/SSRS polls show that voters are increasingly clear about what they want. And President Donald Trump can't or won't give it to them.

The country craves economic relief . People think groceries and the roofs over their heads are too expensive. The vise tightened Thursday when mortgage rates rose above 7%.

With their wages disappearing more quickly, Americans are even more angry about one of the top causes — the Iran war . Even GOP voters are increasing losing confidence in the conflict amid soaring gasoline and diesel prices.

And citizens are increasingly fearful about advances in artificial intelligence . That's no wonder after recent warnings from tech chiefs that their brainchild could threaten humanity.

Yet on this trio of issues, and many others, Trump is offering a program that is exactly opposite of what most Americans want.

He's evoking an economic "golden age" which only he can see. He insists, falsely, that he's bought food prices way down . As for inflation, it's the fault of Joe Biden — who left the presidency 19 months ago.

This explains Republicans' nightmare political environment. Only 27% in a CNN/SSRS survey this week expressed confidence in Trump's handling of the economy. A similarly tiny cohort thought that economic conditions are good. Pity vulnerable Republicans, because two-thirds of Americans polled said the economy is "extremely important" to their vote in November.

The CNN polls also show that three-quarters of Americans don't think the president has a plan to exit a war that's about to enter its eighth month. On Wednesday, in a speech at the UN General Assembly, he proved them right. He revealed that he was hovering between an effort to "annihilate" Iran or to make a deal with it. His woolly prediction that the conflict will somehow end after the midterms won't reassure two-thirds of Americans who think the US is not winning. Only 26% approve of his handling of the war.

On AI, Trump has again chosen the side of the issue guaranteed to alienate the largest crop of voters. "I want to leave it exactly where it is," he wrote on social media Thursday. The 7 in 10 Americans who say the government should regulate it more are out of luck.

How Trump could experience the worst of all worlds

Presidents shouldn't do things just because they are popular. Sometimes, tacking away from voters shows principles and courage. Often politicians are accused of looking at the polls, then deciding on a key issue. That's not Trump.

But he does seem to have forgotten that lowering prices and staying out of new wars was key to his appeal in 2024. He's honored a third pillar of his campaign — securing the southern border — but draconian deportation raids may be alienating critical moderate and Hispanic voters.

Consistently taking positions that deny the pain voters feel or refusing to listen to their fears — for instance, that they may lose their jobs to AI — is hardly a recipe for success in a democratic political system. Trump's preference to use his political capital on things he cares about more — like his proposed triumphal arch in Washington — epitomizes his self-referential second term. It suggests he's isolated amid West Wing officials and Cabinet members who shower him in endless public praise.

Midterm elections in a first term often result in a rebuke of a president who's perceived as not living up to his promises, as President Barack Obama found out in 2010. Second-term midterms often dent a presidency running out of steam and reveal an electorate pining for change, as President George W. Bush learned in 2006.

Trump, after winning a nonconsecutive second term following four years out of office, risks experiencing the worst of both these worlds.

For GOP candidates running in a desperate political climate and saddled by a deeply unpopular president, the distinction hardly matters.

Democrats have little to take for granted

The president's determination to make himself the focus of the campaign despite his unpopularity means it's easy for Democratic challengers to pin their incumbent GOP rivals with his record.

Democrat Troy Jackson, running to oust Maine Sen. Susan Collins, warned in July that Republicans take voters for "idiots" when they argue the economy is strong. "We all have eyes, we can see our paychecks and the bills that we have and we know that we are getting screwed and we also know who is to blame," he said.

Sen. Jon Ossoff, seeking reelection in Georgia, has coined snappy phrases to link the war with higher costs. "He promised to lower prices on Day 1, and he also promised peace," Ossoff said at an Atlanta campaign rally, accusing Trump of building a "monument to himself while plunging us deeper into a war he doesn't know how to end or how to win."

Democrats also slam Republicans over vast, power-guzzling AI data centers, painting them as another way Trump's big tech friends profit while regular Americans suffer. "Don't raise our electric bills, don't poison our water, and hire local union labor. If you can't meet that, then get out," Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, who is running for Congress in Pennsylvania, said in a recent campaign ad.

But there are warning signs for Democrats.

In 2026, being anti-Trump may be enough. But polls show the party is yet to win back voters' confidence after its farcical 2024 presidential campaign, when Biden pulled out late and Vice President Kamala Harris lost to Trump.

CNN's latest polling found that voters prefer Democrats over the GOP by 8 points. But that is 4 points less than at the equivalent moment in Trump's first term, ahead of Democrats' recapture of the House in the 2018 midterms. Congressional Democrats are no more popular than their GOP counterparts, with only about one-quarter of Americans registering approval. And while Democrats enjoy a 10-point edge on whether they'd improve health care policy if handed power, voters are split on whether they'd improve the cost of living, citizens' finances, corruption or foreign policy.

This comes against the backdrop of the Democratic Party's quickening ideological battle between progressives and democratic socialists and more moderate members closer to the political center. A narrow Democratic majority in the House or Senate next year could experience a mirror image of the splits that hampered the GOP House's legislative agenda over the last two years.

Polls offer only a current snapshot of opinion. And other factors beyond Iran, AI and the economy could break late in the campaign. Democrats, meanwhile, worry that their lead in the polls must withstand an avalanche of cash from GOP donors and Trump's war chest. And no one can know the true nature of the electorate that will show up until November 3.

Yet Trump's problems are so intractable there's little hope of a quick turnaround for the GOP. And early voting starts in early- and mid-October in many states.

Five weeks out, the country is unhappy with the leadership that it has, and is yet to be convinced that any replacement will ease its fundamental challenges.

articles.title: Unearthed: El-Sayed called for repealing law that made sex without disclosing HIV status a felony
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed once called Michigan's HIV criminalization law "hateful" and "discriminatory," a stance now under scrutiny in his Senate race.
articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed has consistently called for the repeal of a Michigan law that made it a felony for people with HIV to have sex without informing their partner of their status.

El-Sayed, now running for Senate in Michigan, has stood by his position to decriminalize HIV and fight discrimination against those with the disease.

The law was reformed in 2019 with bipartisan support, limiting felony provisions to specific cases and protecting medically suppressed individuals from prosecution.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed once called for repealing a Michigan law that made it a felony for people who knew they had HIV to have sex without first informing their partner — a position he is standing by eight years later as he campaigns in one of the nation's most competitive Senate races

As he unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018, El-Sayed repeatedly took aim at the law. The law carried a prison sentence of up to four years for people who knew they were HIV-positive and engaged in sexual penetration without first informing their partner of their HIV status.

"You should not be criminalized for a disease. That is absolutely wrong. It's hateful. It's discriminatory, and we can, as a state, do better. You can count on me for that," El-Sayed said as he ran for governor.

Fast-forward eight years and El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and a former health director for Detroit-anchored Wayne County, is battling former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the midterm race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The showdown in Michigan is a must hold for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the Senate from the GOP.

As he ran for the 2018 Democratic gubernatorial nomination — a contest he lost to now-two-term Gov. Gretchen Whitmer — El-Sayed's campaign website stated, "Repeal HIV/AIDS criminalization laws and the exclusion of transgender Michiganders from state Medicaid."

When asked in 2018 if he supported the decriminalization of HIV through legislation that would create two levels of misdemeanors, El-Sayed said at the time , "One of the big things that we have to recognize about HIV is that no disease can be illegal. The continuing forward of these laws on the books stigmatize people with the disease."

Whitmer also supported changing the law, which dated to 1988, saying as she ran for governor, "It's wrong to criminalize sickness, which is what this law has effectively done. It absolutely should be revisited."

The law was reformed in early 2019, after passing a GOP-controlled legislature with broad bipartisan support. The revised statute limited the felony provisions to vaginal and anal intercourse involving an intent to transmit HIV or cases in which HIV was actually transmitted, reduced certain non-transmission offenses to misdemeanors and protected medically suppressed people from prosecution under the law's reckless-disregard provision.

"Abdul supports the bipartisan reform bill that passed in 2019 through a Republican legislature that eliminated the discriminatory laws on the books," campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital. "As a public health professional, Abdul has fought to support programs that stem the spread of diseases, including HIV ."

Richner added that "the Trump administration has completely exacerbated this crisis by defunding the organizations and programs that do frontline care to prevent transmission and exposure in the first place. In the US Senate, Abdul will fight back against Donald Trump and RFK Jr's attempts to dismantle our public health infrastructure and ensure all Americans have access to the care they need."

El-Sayed also stands by his past comments on fighting discrimination aimed at those with HIV.

Last week, as he landed an endorsement from the Human Rights Campaign , a leading LGBTQ advocacy group, El-Sayed highlighted that if elected to the Senate, "I'll fight to ensure every Michigander can live without discrimination and never have to wonder whether their rights will still be there tomorrow."

El-Sayed, who narrowly edged more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in August in a contentious primary that further exposed the rift between the party's left-wing and establishment factions, would become the nation's first Muslim senator if elected.

He has made support for "Medicare for all" a major component of his campaign. El-Sayed has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and has been a vocal critic of Israel during its war against Hamas, characterizing Israel's actions in Gaza as "genocide" against Palestinians.

articles.title: Early 2028 primary poll shows clear frontrunners for both parties
articles.summary: A new poll from McLaughlin & Associates shows these two potential candidates leading the way ahead of the 2028 presidential primaries.
articles.body:
With the November midterms only weeks away, some are already looking ahead as buzz around potential 2028 presidential candidates has grown, with new polling showing clear frontrunners for both the GOP and the Democrats.

In a new poll released Thursday, Sept. 24, by McLaughlin & Associates, a showdown between vice presidents could be in the cards, as former Vice President Kamala Harris and current Vice President JD Vance lead their respective hypothetical primaries.

Thursday's poll is the latest 2028 presidential primary poll showing Harris and Vance leading, with other recent polls, including one by YouGov/Bowling Green State University , showing the prospective candidates ahead of their packs.

See 19 potential Democratic presidential candidates for the 2028 election

Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel

According to the poll, Harris leads among Democrats with 29% support. Her nearest challenger, California Gov. Gavin Newsom , came in with 12% support, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 9%; 15% of Democrats polled said they were undecided.

Among Republicans, Vance leads with 35% of primary voters; the battle for second is closer, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 15% and President Donald Trump 's son, Donald Trump Jr. , at 14%; 12% of Republicans said they were undecided.

The poll surveyed 463 likely voters from Sept. 16 to Sept. 22, according to McLaughlin & Associates.

As of Sept. 25, no, but some potential candidates have already seemingly signaled their intentions ahead of 2028.

Earlier this month, Newsom spoke with CNN and said he would not run in 2028 if Harris decided to campaign for the seat a second time. The California governor made the statement during a fishing trip in Montana with CNN's Jake Tapper , after the reporter asked about his presidential ambitions if Harris joined the race.

On the Republican side, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas fueled speculation about another White House bid.

"It's no secret that I want to be president," Cruz said in August on Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick's podcast.

While Cruz signaled his potential to run, Rubio has sought to subdue speculation, although he did not completely rule out a campaign.

"I don't know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time," Rubio said during an official visit to Colombia earlier this month. "I'm not a candidate for anything right now. And I'm 100% focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs."

articles.title: Bill Gates warns AI is 'powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths'
articles.summary: The cofounder of Microsoft made grave predictions about AI and voiced support for government regulation of the sector.
articles.body:
Bill Gates is pro-government regulation of AI companies.

In an upcoming interview with "Meet the Press," Microsoft's cofounder said the tech could "cause a billion deaths."

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has urged the AI industry to prioritize safety.

Bill Gates has some serious fears about how AI can be misused.

The cofounder of Microsoft made grave warnings about the tech in an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," saying that "AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths."

Gates also said that the industry needs government regulation. "You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like," he said.

Gates' comments echo those of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who said in a September essay calling on frontier AI companies to slow down development that the "most effective method of pacing is via regulation."

In a clip of the "Meet the Press" published on Thursday ahead of the full interview on Sunday, Gates said he worries about bad actors getting their hands on advanced AI tools. Anthropic recently published a report detailing several instances where state and non-state actors used Claude to plan drone attacks and for dangerous biological research.

Amodei's essay calling for AI pacing, which received support from Elon Musk and Sam Altman, was published in the wake of warnings from ex-Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon , who wrote a viral post about resigning and AI labs "gambling with our lives."

The AI safety warnings have so far failed to convince Washington that development of the tech should be paused or slowed down. President Donald Trump, for his part, mocked Amodei, accusing him of "pretending to be a 'perfect little angel.'" Trump has signaled strong disinterest in regulating AI, though he did pledge last week to create an " AI Force " that would "watch over" AI companies.

Even Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO and chairman, has appeared reticent to call for all-out regulation of the tech. In a recent appearance on the All-In Podcast, Nadella said AI companies should handle things on their own.

"If you see a show-stopper," Nadella said, referring to anomalies in code that could produce rogue AI agents, "stop the show."

Though there is broad agreement across Silicon Valley that AI companies should implement more robust safeguards to protect against incidents like OpenAI's breach of Hugging Face, CEOs differ on how such safeguards should be enforced.

This month, Nadella warned in a memo to Microsoft employees viewed by Business Insider that companies must take time to make the technology safe.

Gates, who now serves as a technology advisor to Nadella and other Microsoft executives, was previously one of AI's most outspoken optimists before changing course over the summer.

In an essay he published in August, Gates said the world has no plan to roll out AI safely.

"I believe we need time to prepare for the period of social, political, and economic upheaval we are about to enter," he said. "If someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it."

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects a Trump-backed Missouri congressional map for the third time
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by President Donald Trump, putting an end to a long-running...
articles.body:
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — The Supreme Court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by President Donald Trump, putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is underway in the midterm elections.

The justices halted a federal appeals court ruling that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November elections, which will determine control of Congress. There were no noted dissents.

The Supreme Court instead let stand a decision by the Missouri Supreme Court , which ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new map from being used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. The decision means Missouri residents will vote under the same congressional districts used in the 2024 and 2022 elections.

"At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos," the high court wrote in an unsigned opinion. "The District Court and Court of Appeals should not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri."

Republicans had hoped the new House map — which already was used in the August primaries — could help them win an additional seat as part of a nationwide redistricting battle pushed by Trump to gain an edge in the midterms.

The new map had targeted a district held by longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

"I think my reelection prospects shot up significantly," a jubilant Cleaver said after the Supreme Court ruling.

A panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had ruled Monday that switching districts between the primary and general elections would violate the U.S. Constitution. The panel directed a district judge to bar Missouri from using anything other than the new map but delayed the order's effect until next Monday to allow time for an appeal to the Supreme Court.

The legal wrangling has caused confusion for more than a million potential Missouri voters — nearly 1 in 4 statewide — who were shifted from one district to another, resulting in different candidates on their ballots. Absentee voting began Tuesday under the 2022 congressional districts. Thousands of ballots already had been mailed, and some already have been cast.

A decision from the Supreme Court is "a big sigh of relief," said Kansas City election director Shawn Kieffer. He added, "We just want it over, so we can do our job properly."

Republican redistricting focused on Kansas City

Republicans currently hold six of Missouri's eight House districts. At the urging of Trump and Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers last September passed revised districts that were intended to help them win seven seats in the midterms.

The redistricting significantly reshaped a Kansas City-based district held by Cleaver. It shed parts of Kansas City to neighboring districts with Republican incumbents and stretched the remainder of Cleaver's 5th Congressional District far eastward into rural Republican areas.

The result was about 59% of potential voters were new to the district, according to an Associated Press estimate. The ripple effects also shifted some voters in most of Missouri's other congressional districts.

Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. Republican state Sen. Rick Brattin won a six-way Republican primary under the revised districts. They remain the candidates for the general election, even though the district boundaries have reverted to their prior lines.

Cleaver said the court ruling affirms the people's right to use to referendum petitions against state legislative actions they don't like.

"We just received a healthy dose of encouragement that the voice of people in the United States still matters," he said.

Brattin was a plaintiff, along with Republican Rep. Bob Onder and two other voters, in a federal lawsuit that led to the 8th Circuit's ruling and the last two appeals to the Supreme Court. He had no immediate comment.

Missouri's redistricting prompted a big legal fight

At least 16 lawsuits have been filed in state and federal courts related to Missouri's congressional redistricting. The battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their U.S. House districts over the past year.

Missouri's new map survived most of the lawsuits, including ones contending that mid-decade redistricting violated the state constitution and that the new districts ran afoul of requirements to be compact . In one case, the Missouri Supreme Court allowed the new districts to be used while election officials worked to verify petition signatures seeking to put the map to a statewide vote.

Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins waited until the legal deadline on Aug. 4 — the day the new districts were used in the primaries — to reject the petition . He asserted referendum petitions aren't allowed for congressional redistricting.

The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Sept. 3 that the referendum petition was valid. It ordered Hoskins not to use the new map and to instead use the districts adopted in 2022, after the last census. The U.S. Supreme Court let that ruling stand on Sept. 8. But minutes later, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting order in favor of the new map.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Sept. 10 blocked Clark's order from taking effect. That day, the Missouri Supreme Court held Hoskins temporarily in contempt for telling local election authorities to use the new map after Clark's order.

But that wasn't the end of the matter. The 8th Circuit, hearing an appeal of Clark's blocked order, ruled in favor of the Trump-backed map Monday. That's what led to the latest decision from the U.S. Supreme Court.

Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said the group was pressing forward with its campaign to persuade voters to permanently reject the new map in the November referendum.

"We have said from the beginning, people, not politicians will be the final deciders on this DC power grab," he said in a statement.

Associated Press writer Lindsay Whitehurst in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters
articles.summary: Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada
articles.body:
The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words " Lake America ".

In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized "for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused".

Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family's sweaters to say Lake America , which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US's federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president's trade war with Canada.

Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: "Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will."

The post ended with "Lol lol". It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.

Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News .

Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax's role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.

As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.

"We weren't trying to make a political statement," Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT . "However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun" at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.

"I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry," she continued in her remarks to WJRT. "I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.

"I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don't value them as human beings."

Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.

"Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately," said a statement from the organization shared on social media.

After saying Smith's interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, "We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.

"We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first."

Family First Credit Union's statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump's executive order changing Lake Ontario's name to Lake America.

Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water's name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US's declaration of independence from the UK.

"Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always," he wrote on X.

Several US governors in the US's Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.

The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.

Trump's order has no authority to rename Canada's portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada , international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.
