articles.body:
Após o fim do debate entre os candidatos ao Senado pelo Acre, realizado na noite desta sexta-feira (25) pela Rede Amazônica Acre, os três participantes fizeram uma breve avaliação do confronto. Estiveram presentes Eduardo Velloso (Solidariedade), Jorge Viana (PT) e Inácio Moreira (PSOL).

O debate foi o primeiro realizado para candidatos ao Senado e teve como temas saúde, bioeconomia, indústria, tecnologia e casos de corrupção, além de críticas à ausência dos candidatos convidados que não participaram do confronto.

Gladson Cameli (PP), Marcio Bittar (PL), Mara Rocha (Republicanos) e Sérgio Petecão (PSD) foram convidados, mas recusaram a participação.

O confronto foi mediado pelo jornalista Fabiano Villela, da TV Globo, e transmitido pelo g1 Acre e rádio CBN Amazônia Rio Branco.

Candidatos ao Senado pelo Acre participam de debate na Rede Amazônica — Foto: Arquivo g1

Jorge Viana (PT) afirmou que ficou satisfeito com a oportunidade de apresentar sua trajetória e defender propostas para o estado. O candidato citou a experiência como prefeito de Rio Branco, governador e senador e disse que pretende voltar ao Senado para, segundo ele, ajudar a enfrentar o momento vivido pelo Acre.

"São duas vagas para senador, eu estou pedindo um voto, eu estou pondo a minha vida, a minha história, a minha experiência de ex-prefeito, ex-governador, ex-senador, porque o Acre está vivendo um momento terrível. A população está sofrendo muito, alguns indo embora. Eu não quero o Acre assim, eu quero o Acre voltando a dar certo, por isso que eu estou aqui, vindo, estou muito contente e esperando que as pessoas me ajudem a cuidar do Acre novamente", frisou.

Eduardo Velloso (Solidariedade) destacou a discussão sobre saúde durante o debate. Médico e deputado federal, ele afirmou que pretende levar a experiência acumulada na área para o Senado e citou ações que, segundo ele, contribuíram para melhorar o atendimento no interior.

"Foi muito importante para dialogar e mostrar para a população quem realmente tem compromisso com o estado do Acre. Eu sou o único representante da saúde, estou preparado. Já fizemos, como deputado, uma grande mudança na saúde, melhoramos a vida, principalmente das pessoas do interior", destacou.

Já Professor Inácio Moreira (PSOL) ressaltou a oportunidade de participar de um debate com ampla audiência. O candidato, que se apresenta como representante da periferia, afirmou que o espaço permite discutir problemas que, segundo ele, não são vivenciados pelos políticos mais ricos.

"Eu acho que a lição que fica pra gente, que é da periferia, que a gente pode. Você, independente se você vai ter um tostão ou um milhão, tem que participar desse processo da democracia, dar sua opinião pra falarmos do mundo real que a gente vive porque esses políticos milionários não conhecem a nossa realidade, eles moram em condomínio e eles falam nos outdoors de bilhões e bilhões que não chegam no nosso bairro", comentou.

articles.title: VÍDEO: Por que existem duas casas no Congresso? | G1
articles.standfirst: As duas Casas precisam aprovar leis, mas também podem participar de etapas diferentes de um mesmo processo. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: As duas Casas precisam aprovar leis, mas também podem participar de etapas diferentes de um mesmo processo. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.body:
Câmara e Senado participam da elaboração das leis, mas representam interesses diferentes dentro do Congresso Nacional.

A Câmara representa a população brasileira. Por isso, estados mais populosos elegem mais deputados federais do que estados com menos habitantes . São Paulo, por exemplo, tem 70 cadeiras na Câmara, enquanto Roraima tem oito.

No Senado, a lógica é diferente. Cada estado e o Distrito Federal têm exatamente três senadores, independentemente do tamanho da população. Na prática, isso significa que um estado pequeno tem o mesmo número de representantes que um estado grande na Casa.

A ideia é equilibrar as duas formas de representação: a da população e a dos estados. E o sistema com duas Casas também funciona como uma espécie de revisão das propostas que tramitam no Congresso.

📍 Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 vai explicar os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

Por isso, para que um projeto se transforme em lei, ele precisa passar pelas duas Casas. Câmara e Senado analisam e votam as propostas e, dependendo de onde o projeto começou, a outra Casa pode revisar o texto antes que ele siga para sanção ou promulgação.

Esse processo faz com que uma mesma proposta passe por duas instâncias de deliberação, com deputados e senadores participando de etapas diferentes da sua tramitação.

Em alguns casos, as duas Casas também participam de momentos diferentes de um mesmo processo.

➡️É a Câmara, por exemplo, que pode autorizar a abertura de processos de impeachment contra o presidente da República. O julgamento desses processos cabe ao Senado.

➡️O Senado também analisa e aprova ou rejeita indicações feitas pelo presidente da República para cargos como ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e outras autoridades.

É por isso que existem duas Casas no Congresso: elas representam a população e os estados de formas diferentes, participam da elaboração das leis e também exercem funções de revisão e atribuições próprias.

articles.title: WATCH: Former Dem Lt Gov reveals why he resigned after sexual harassment probe rocked state
articles.summary: Dale Caldwell called the ethics probe "specious" and "poorly done" on camera, insisting he resigned only to avoid distracting Gov. Mikie Sherrill.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Former New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell insisted on camera Friday that he resigned "to make a difference" rather than impede Gov. Mikie Sherrill, while directly disputing the findings of a sexual harassment and ethics probe that forced him from office. Caldwell’s departure came just one day after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill publicly called for his resignation following a months-long independent ethics investigation. The 61-page report described repeated ethics violations, including a "substantiated" finding of sexual harassment and repeated improper efforts to secure a state job promotion for a woman with whom he was romantically involved. Speaking on camera for the first time since his resignation to a reporter outside his home, Caldwell slammed the state's investigative report as "specious," "ridiculous" and "poorly done," adding he resigned to keep any "distraction" away from the Sherrill administration. "I'm not resigning because of that ridiculous report," Caldwell said on camera. "I'm resigning because I don't want to be a distraction to the Mikie Sherrill administration. HOUSE DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATED OVER ALLEGED 'INAPPROPRIATE SEXUAL CONTACT' WITH STAFFER "If I'm going to impede anybody else's ability to be successful, then I can move on to something else," Caldwell added, citing his history as a university president and working at the Deloitte consulting firm. When pressed about the allegations in the report, Caldwell encouraged people to go read it for themselves but said he was only providing specifics through his attorney for now. "I just think it was poorly done. It was poorly done. I mean, I just think that there are ways that they could have done better. And I was just disappointed in the legal, the legal work in that," Caldwell added. GOP LAWMAKER'S GIFTS, 'EFFUSIVE AFFECTION' TOWARD YOUNG STAFFERS DETAILED IN EXPLOSIVE ETHICS REPORT Caldwell also mentioned that he spoke with Gov. Sherrill via text message Friday, noting "she's a wonderful person" and "she really means well" but did not provide any more specifics on that conversation. "This is one of those things that happens. And as I said, I'm going to continue to work as a private citizen," Caldwell said. "I'm freed up to do a lot more things. So, I'm looking forward to supporting the administration and really supporting folks." According to the probe into Caldwell's behavior, conducted by an independent law firm hired by the state, Caldwell violated ethics rules after telling a female staffer that "you young women are looking for young sperm" after she told him her younger friend was not interested in a romantic relationship with him. Investigators concluded the remark constituted sexual harassment and found Caldwell’s denial that he made it was not credible. Other findings from the probe included violations of the code of conduct and ethics around bringing guests to ticketed events without reimbursement and seeking a promotion for a state employee with whom he had a romantic relationship. FORMER TRUMP CABINET OFFICIAL HAD 'INAPPROPRIATELY CLOSE' RELATIONSHIP WITH BODYGUARD, IG FINDS Lawyers for Caldwell said Thursday they "strongly disputed the three findings in the investigation" because its conclusions "go further than the evidence supports," according to NBC News. But Sherrill pushed back on the criticism from Thomas Calcagni, Caldwell's lawyer, of the investigation, saying she thought it was "very thorough," adding it "lays out exactly what the investigation looked into, who they contacted and spoke to, and I think lays out a pattern and practice of long-term concerning behavior." She also called the claims of sexual harassment "substantiated" and said Caldwell continued to violate standards despite "multiple" violations and ethics trainings. Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey’s secretary of state, heading an office that oversees elections. Sherrill said Friday that the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, would become acting secretary of state with just weeks to go until the midterm elections. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under the New Jersey State Constitution, a vacancy in the office of the lieutenant governor must be permanently filled by the governor within 45 days. Addressing the transition, Sherrill confirmed she will appoint a permanent successor within that constitutionally mandated 45-day window but stated she does not plan to name an acting lieutenant governor in the interim. Without an interim lieutenant governor in place, the line of gubernatorial succession falls to Senate President Nicholas Scutari in the event of an emergency or if Sherrill leaves the state before a permanent appointment is made.

articles.title: TikTok settles for over $100 million in mental health lawsuit, Alabama AG says
articles.summary: The Alabama Attorney General’s Office announced Friday it reached a minimum $100 million settlement deal with TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance, days before a state court was set to hear arguments surrounding the app’s potential mental health effects on minors. TikTok has 45 days to respond to the settlement, which could balloon to $300…
articles.body:
The Alabama Attorney General’s Office announced Friday it reached a minimum $100 million settlement deal with TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance, days before a state court was set to hear arguments surrounding the app’s potential mental health effects on minors.

TikTok has 45 days to respond to the settlement , which could balloon to $300 million if certain conditions are met. The move marks the first time the social media platform has settled as it engages in several similar legal battles related to the wellbeing of its minor users, according to Reuters .

In addition to the payment, the agreement also requires that TikTok implement a host of safety features designed to protect children using its platform — including daily time limits, stronger content moderation, more user-friendly parental controls and a blanket prohibition on cosmetic filters by teen users.

It also mandates that the app add “productive pauses” that interrupt teen users after 15, 60 and 90 minutes of continuous use “to limit endless scrolling.”

The app will also add nighttime restrictions as a result of the settlement, restricting children’s access to TikTok from 12:00 a.m. to 6:00 a.m. and placing blocks on notifications during this period. The settlement says the platform must add similar restrictions during school hours.

Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall’s office accused the company last year of making its platform purposefully addictive for young users and negatively impacted the wellbeing of teenagers in the state.

TikTok has defended itself in the past by saying it designed the platform with teen safety in mind, which a federal judge ruled against.

“This is a great day for Alabama parents. Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction. TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app,” Marshall wrote in a press release about the settlement deal.

When asked about the settlement, a TikTok U.S. Data Security Joint Venture spokesperson told The Hill, “TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community.”

“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson continued.

articles.title: Fulton Sheen became a TV sensation preaching faith, morality and warnings Michael Knowles says still resonate
articles.summary: Conservative commentator says famous Catholic archbishop would be branded a "far-right extremist" today without changing his message on faith and communism.
articles.body: Archbishop Fulton Sheen drew tens of millions of Americans to their TV sets with little more than a chalkboard, a cape and a message about Christianity, morality and the threat of communism. More than seven decades later, conservative commentator Michael Knowles said he believes the legendary Catholic broadcaster could deliver essentially the same message and immediately find himself branded a "far-right extremist." "I think he would be taking his first breath to utter the first syllable of the very first sentence just when someone called him a far-right extremist," Knowles told Fox News Digital. "He wouldn't need to change his message." BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE REAL REASON COMMUNISTS FEAR RELIGION AND WANT BELIEVERS SILENCED Sheen was formally beatified, or formally "blessed" by the Roman Catholic Church Thursday in St. Louis, marking a major step toward possible sainthood for one of the most recognizable religious figures of 20th century America. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump joined Catholics celebrating Sheen's life, the White House called him the first American-born bishop to be beatified by the Catholic Church. Long before podcasts and social media gave religious figures direct access to enormous audiences, Sheen became one of America's most successful religious broadcasters. His radio program, "The Catholic Hour," reached more than 4 million people, according to Vatican News. He later made the leap to television, where "Life Is Worth Living" eventually captivated an estimated 30 million viewers. The format was strikingly simple. AMERICA HAS FOUNDING FATHERS A CATHOLIC SAINT WAS A FOUNDING MOTHER Wearing his clerical robes and standing before a chalkboard, Sheen spoke directly to viewers about faith, morality, suffering and the dignity of the human person, weaving theology with stories and humor. "He was the very first televangelist," said Knowles, who argued Sheen understood something about mass communication that remains true in the digital age. "He went where the people were." Sheen's reach extended far beyond a conventional religious audience. The White House also noted that he competed with entertainment giants Milton Berle and Frank Sinatra in weekly ratings, appeared on the cover of Time magazine and won an Emmy for outstanding television personality. CHASTITY BEFORE MARRIAGE? NO COHABITATION? DATA SAYS COUPLES WHO SKIP BOTH MAY HAVE STRONGER UNIONS Among the millions of Americans who encountered Sheen through television was a boy who would eventually become the first American pope. Pope Leo XIV has recalled encountering Sheen's evangelization while growing up. Decades later, Leo approved Sheen's beatification in St. Louis. Knowles said Sheen would likely have embraced podcasts, social media and other modern platforms with the same enthusiasm. But the message delivered through those platforms, Knowles argued, could put Sheen at odds with parts of modern American culture. Asked what would get the bishop "canceled" first in 2026, his Catholicism, his anti-communism or his refusal to apologize for either, Knowles said the three were difficult to separate. "His absolutely unapologetic apologetics," Knowles said. Knowles argued that Sheen's traditional Catholic teachings about sex, marriage and human nature would draw particularly fierce criticism today. "They would have tried to cancel him," Knowles said, before adding that Sheen would ultimately have "the last laugh in heaven." Sheen's opposition to communism was central to his public ministry and was emphasized by the White House as Americans marked his beatification. The presidential message described Sheen as bringing Christian teaching to a world "threatened by the titanic forces of communism." The White House also recalled Sheen warning in the 1960s about what he described as a destructive impulse sweeping American society. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE WAR ON CHRISTIANS IS REAL, AND THE WORLD CAN NO LONGER STAY SILENT "Our nation is too full of those that are crying, ‘Down,'" Sheen said in the remarks shared by the White House, before listing schools, churches, teachers, government and police. "Can you build anything down?" Knowles said Sheen's warnings continue to resonate because the underlying debate about human nature has not disappeared in modern times. He tied the recurring appeal of communist and utopian political movements to the Christian doctrine of original sin, arguing that political systems fail when they begin from a mistaken conception of human nature. "When their policies are implemented, they fail," Knowles said. Yet Sheen's journey to Thursday's beatification ultimately rests not on his television ratings or political commentary, but on the Catholic Church's assessment of his religious life and a miracle attributed to his intercession. His cause for sainthood opened in Peoria, Illinois, in 2002. The miracle accepted for Sheen's beatification centered on a child born in 2010 without a heartbeat or respiration, according to an account published by Vatican News. After 61 minutes, the child was revived and ultimately recovered to full health. Pope Francis approved the miracle in 2019, clearing a major hurdle in Sheen's path toward beatification. The Catholic Church's recognition of Sheen was not presented merely as a celebration of his TV celebrity. Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, who represented Pope Leo at Thursday's beatification Mass, emphasized Sheen's relationship with Christ and missionary work rather than his fame. In an apostolic letter read during the ceremony, Leo described Sheen as an evangelist who used modern communications to proclaim the Gospel. Sheen's connections to the modern papacy stretch much further back. He participated in the Second Vatican Council, where, according to a biography published by Vatican News, he encountered two clerics who would eventually become popes: Archbishop Karol Wojtyla, the future Pope John Paul II, and Father Joseph Ratzinger, the future Pope Benedict XVI. Shortly before Sheen's death, his path crossed John Paul II's again. During the pope's 1979 visit to New York, a physically weakened Sheen approached John Paul at St. Patrick's Cathedral and attempted to kneel before him. John Paul lifted him up and embraced him, according to the Vatican account. "You have written and spoken well of the Lord Jesus Christ," John Paul told him. "You are a loyal son of the Church." Sheen died just two months later on Dec. 9, 1979. For Knowles, however, Sheen's ability to draw an enormous audience wasn't simply a product of theology or the novelty of television. "He took life seriously. He just didn't take himself seriously," Knowles said. That combination allowed Sheen to tackle weighty subjects without becoming ponderous, Knowles argued, and helped make complex religious and philosophical arguments accessible to an audience far beyond practicing Catholics. People might discover Sheen through his anti-communism position, cultural traditionalism or even an appreciation for formal dress among people tired of seeing "sweatpants at the airport," Knowles joked. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But beneath the television celebrity and political commentary was a priest who maintained a daily Holy Hour before the Eucharist throughout his ministry, a practice Sheen called "the hour that makes my day," according to the Vatican News biography. Admiring Sheen is one thing, Knowles suggested, but following his example is another. "It would be far better for you and for all of us to follow his example," Knowles said.

articles.title: Trump Rejects Iran Ceasefire, Expects Bombing to Resume After Midterms
articles.summary: Trump Rejects Iran Ceasefire, Expects Bombing to Resume After Midterms
articles.body:
President Trump rejects Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and expects U.S. bombing of Iran to resume after midterm elections.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's proposal to halt hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and restart nuclear negotiations is rejected by Trump.

U.S. and Iranian officials engage in indirect diplomatic contacts during the United Nations General Assembly, exploring a phased arrangement for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting economic blockade.

President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and told aides he expects U.S. bombing of Iran to resume after the November midterm elections, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The Journal, citing U.S. officials, reported Friday that Trump has turned down Tehran's proposal, which would halt hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart negotiations over Iran's nuclear program.

Under the proposal outlined by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz at the end of a seven-day period if Washington agreed to a series of conditions, including lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observing a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

Araghchi said Thursday that Iran had presented the plan to the United States through intermediaries and that implementation could begin once Washington accepted the terms.

The New York Times reported Friday that the proposal closely mirrors a memorandum of understanding reached by the United States and Iran in June but subsequently unraveled, although the new plan compresses the timetable for moving toward nuclear negotiations.

The latest proposal came as U.S. and Iranian officials have renewed indirect diplomatic contacts in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.

Reuters reported Thursday that U.S. and Iranian negotiators were exploring a phased arrangement under which Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz while Washington lifted its economic blockade of Iran.

The talks have included U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, meeting with Araghchi through Qatari mediation, according to the New York Times.

The New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a roughly three-hour meeting mediated by Qatar did not produce a breakthrough, although Iranian officials described the discussions as productive and said further contacts remained possible.

Trump has continued to say that he expects the conflict to be resolved after the midterm elections.

Axios reported Tuesday that Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that he expected the United States and Iran to reach a deal after the elections, while warning that he could instead take more aggressive military action.

Trump has previously said the war could end immediately after the midterms, according to CBS News.

The Journal's latest report goes further, saying Trump has told aides he expects U.S. bombing to resume after the elections, a prospect that would leave open the possibility of a renewed major military campaign if diplomacy fails.

Axios had previously reported that some U.S. officials believed Trump could return to major combat operations after the midterms if no agreement with Tehran was reached, while Trump had declined to say whether he would make the decision before or after the elections.

Iran, meanwhile, has pressed for a deal before the November vote.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that Tehran wanted an agreement before the U.S. midterm elections, while Araghchi said the seven-day proposal could provide a path toward reopening the strategic waterway and restarting comprehensive nuclear negotiations.

The Strait of Hormuz has become a central issue in the diplomacy because it is a major route for global energy shipments, and the conflict has disrupted oil flows and contributed to higher energy prices.

Reuters reported earlier this week that Iran had offered to reopen the strait within seven days if the United States eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports.

Newsmax also reported Friday on Iran's seven-day proposal, including Tehran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear negotiations, as Washington weighs whether diplomacy can produce an agreement without further military action.

articles.title: White House bans CNN from Air Force One for Trump trip to Tennessee
articles.summary: Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House last week, calling them ‘fake news’
articles.body:
CNN reporters have been banned from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee, despite a judge’s order restoring their access to the White House after being previously banned.

The White House announced in a Friday night note that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville for a college football game, leaving major networks unable to televise his trip.

Despite being allowed to cover some events, CNN reporters were stopped from covering Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner, raising concerns about continued access to daily events.

The White House has banned CNN reporters from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee , the network says.

Despite a judge's order restoring CNN's access to the White House after Trump banned the network , along with MS NOW and Politico, from covering his daily activities, reporters are still being denied entry to certain events.

In the latest roadblock, the White House announced in a Friday night note detailing the president's schedule that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville on Saturday for a college football game, the network reported .

CNN is part of a rotating press pool that covers White House events for major TV networks. No other outlet was listed to replace CNN in the memo, according to the network. Without a designated pooler, major networks won't be able to televise his trip.

The network's journalists were also stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to cover Chinese President Xi Jinping's arrival at the White House for a state dinner Thursday night, the network reported .

The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that it could cover the greeting ceremony but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.

MS NOW also reported being blocked from the greeting ceremony. "The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?" MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López asked network host Symone Sanders Townsend Thursday night.

But CNN was allowed to cover Trump and Xi's visit to the National Archives in Washington, D.C., on Friday.

The Independent has reached out to the White House and CNN for comment about the network's coverage of Trump's Knoxville trip.

Coverage of the White House has been spotty ever since Trump banned the three networks last Friday, calling them "fake news."

"Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social.

The outlets then sued to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.

In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets' press badges.

But reporters were still denied entry later Thursday morning. By Thursday afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House.

The White House TV press pool had abstained from filming in solidarity with the outlets Trump banned until their access was reinstated. CBS served as the designated pooler Friday, filming Xi and Trump at the White House during the final day of his state visit .

Trump's disdain for the mainstream press is well-documented, including his outbursts at female journalists for asking questions about the Epstein files and the Iran war. He has repeatedly targeted CNN's Chief White House Correspondent Kaitlan Collins for "not smiling."

But his attempt to ban several major outlets from the White House is unprecedented.

Former President Bill Clinton — who had an affair with a young staffer, Monica Lewinsky , in the 1990s that dominated the news cycle — said at the Clinton Global Initiative summit earlier this week, "There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.

"And there's a reason we have a Constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off."

articles.title: Trump rescinds nearly $1B in federal funding, bypassing congressional approval
articles.summary: President Trump cancelled almost $1 billion in federal funding Friday using the controversial “pocket rescission” process, which allows him to sidestep congressional approval. Most of the cancellations targeted Health and Human Services (HHS) programs serving undocumented immigrants and unaccompanied children in court, as well as similar initiatives under the agency’s Minority Health office and the…
articles.body:
President Trump cancelled almost $1 billion in federal funding Friday using the controversial “pocket rescission” process, which allows him to sidestep congressional approval.

Most of the cancellations targeted Health and Human Services (HHS) programs serving undocumented immigrants and unaccompanied children in court, as well as similar initiatives under the agency’s Minority Health office and the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students.

“These funds previously went to pro-illegal immigration programs and Non-Governmental Organizations that provided services to refugees, asylees, and other non-citizens and put unaccompanied children in harm’s way ,” the White House wrote in a press release .

The release continued, “Thanks to President Trump’s successful border policies, the illegal alien invasion is over and there are fewer people crossing our border than ever before.”

The White House went on to say the decrease in border crossings meant funding toward these programs became excessive, warranting their recission

Other cuts aligned with Trump’s anti-DEI agenda — with the president rescinding funds for HHS gender-affirming care research, minority business development and the Department of Justice’s Community Relations Services, which the White House said promoted identity-conscious law enforcement practices. The administration described these initiatives as “wasteful and harmful.”

The president canceled the $810 million in federal funds through a pocket recession, which “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office .

In response to Trump’s cancellations, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), chair of the Appropriations Committee, called the move — and his use of the recission process — “unlawful.” She also called on the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to spend all of the $1.3 billion appropriated from fiscal 2025 as intended.

“This move shows that OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law,” Collins wrote on social media. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”

The Impoundment Control Act (ICA) lays out rules governing the rescissions process. It allows the administration to temporarily withhold funding for 45 days while Congress considers the rescissions request. If lawmakers opt not to approve the request, the funds must be released.

A pocket rescission occurs when the president sends the same type of request to Congress within 45 days of the end of the fiscal year. Because the request is so late, the funding is essentially paused until it runs out at the end of the year regardless of congressional action.

Collins emphasized that the GAO has already concluded that pocket rescissions are unlawful under the ICA.

“Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law,” she continued.

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), ranking member of the Senate Budget Committee, echoed Collins — similarly condemned Trump’s use of the pocket rescission in a statement. He slammed the president, as well as OMB Director Russell Vought, for the decision, saying they “violated the law by sending Congress more illegal pocket rescissions in the dark of night.”

“The law is not a suggestion, and the President is not a king,” he concluded.

Trump last used the tactic in 2025 to unilaterally cut roughly $5 billion in congressionally approved funding. The Supreme Court agreed at the time to allow the Trump administration to keep the money that was set to expire the next week.

articles.summary: CNN reported its journalists have been barred from joining the press pool traveling with President Trump this weekend. They were set to board Air Force One Saturday to cover his visit to Knoxville for a college football game. The outlet had been scheduled to serve as this weekend’s TV press pooler — a rotating group…
articles.body:
CNN reported its journalists have been barred from joining the press pool traveling with President Trump this weekend. They were set to board Air Force One Saturday to cover his visit to Knoxville for a college football game.

The outlet had been scheduled to serve as this weekend’s TV press pooler — a rotating group of journalists who cover Trump when space is limited and share information with other networks. But the White House announced Friday in a note to the press that CNN would no longer fill this role — the latest swipe in President Trump’s ongoing media outlet ban dispute.

The note did not list another outlet replacing CNN. If the White House doesn’t replace the network with another, there would be no television pool coverage of Trump’s Tennessee visit.

“That’s the system that allows the networks to share video of the president with the whole country. If they aren’t there, the pool can’t function,” Jacqui Heinrich, a Fox anchor and president of the White House Correspondents’ Association president, told CNN.

The move comes after Trump attempted to ban CNN, along with MS NOW and Politico, from accessing the White House earlier this week. A federal judge ordered the administration to immediately restore press credentials for reporters at the outlets, finding that the ban likely violated their constitutional due process rights.

On Thursday, journalists attempting to enter the White House grounds were initially denied entry before being allowed onto the grounds in the afternoon.

MS NOW and CNN journalists also reported Thursday they were denied access to the state dinner arrival at the White House during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the U.S., which was a precredentialed event.

The dispute caused the other four major TV news networks — CBS, ABC, NBC and Fox News — to boycott the press pool in solidarity with CNN, which had previously been in the rotation. Though the judge’s ruling came Thursday, these outlets didn’t return until a day later, saying they wanted to be sure the White House would acknowledge the decision when it came to TV coverage.

articles.title: New York, New Jersey declare states of emergency ahead of nor’easter
articles.summary: The governors of New York, Kathy Hochul (D), and New Jersey, Mikie Sherrill (D), both announced Friday they would declare states of emergency ahead of this weekend’s nor’easter. “I’m declaring a State of Emergency for Nassau, Suffolk, New York City and Westchester as this powerful coastal storm bears down on the region,” Hochul wrote on…
articles.body:
The governors of New York, Kathy Hochul (D), and New Jersey, Mikie Sherrill (D), both announced Friday they would declare states of emergency ahead of this weekend’s nor’easter.

“I’m declaring a State of Emergency for Nassau, Suffolk, New York City and Westchester as this powerful coastal storm bears down on the region,” Hochul wrote on social media Friday afternoon. “We’re expecting dangerous coastal flooding, strong winds and potential power outages through the weekend.”

Later in the evening, Sherrill placed New Jersey’s Atlantic, Burlington, Cape May, Cumberland, Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean and Salem counties in a state of emergency.

“I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert, and follow local guidance. We’re prepared and will keep you updated as conditions develop,” she Sherill wrote on social media .

In Manasquan, a borough on the coast of New Jersey, officials recommended residents voluntary evacuate, according to a local NBC affiliate . The recommendations specifically targeted residents in low-lying zones, especially those who are elderly and individuals with special needs.

As the storm approaches, The Weather Channel reported wind gusts over 30 miles per hour along the coast of the Empire State and the Garden State on Friday, stretching down to parts of North Carolina. In Long Island, windspeeds reached up to 52 miles per hour.

The National Weather Service forecasted moderate to locally major flooding over the weekend, particularly in several New York City counties — prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani to issue a statement encouraging residents to get ready for the nor’easter.

“The storm’s expected path has shifted closer to our city, bringing heavier rain and stronger winds,” Mamdani wrote.

After giving tips for how to stay safe during the storm, he concluded, “Look out for your neighbors.”

articles.title: Lawmakers slam Trump’s ‘unlawful’ move to cut $810 million in federal funds
articles.summary: The White House said Friday that it planned to cut $810 million in bipartisan, congressionally approved funding, spurring criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.
articles.body: The White House said Friday that it planned to cut $810 million in bipartisan, congressionally approved funding, spurring criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. The executive branch would effectively send the funds back to Congress using so-called pocket rescissions, a rare budgetary tactic that the Trump administration has used before to negate congressionally allocated spending. The rejected funding affects several programs and agencies serving immigrants, minority groups and Department of Health and Human Services research programs. The administration has argued that while the law gives Congress a 45-day period to accept or reject a White House decision to withhold funds, there is no way to follow that protocol if the action occurs less than 45 days before the end of the fiscal year. That argument has been challenged in court and criticized by lawyers and both Republican and Democratic lawmakers. The fiscal year ends Sept. 30, only a few days away, and the House is not scheduled to return until after the midterm elections in November. The White House announced the move in a statement Friday, describing the rejected funding as “the most harmful government spending.” “President Trump is committed to utilizing all possible tools to cut wasteful and harmful government spending that does not benefit American citizens,” the statement said. Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, called the administration’s move “unlawful” Friday and said, “I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.” “This move shows that [the Office of Management and Budget] intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law,” Collins wrote in a statement. “Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers.” She wrote that as OMB is part of the executive branch, “It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., who serves as vice chair of the Appropriations Committee, called the move a “theft from the American people” and took aim at OMB Director Russ Vought. “Russ Vought’s message to Congress is that your votes don’t count, and your laws are optional,” Murray said in a statement. “It is now time for my Republican colleagues who said they would never let this happen to stand up and join us to stop this, and remind this administration this is not how this works.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., also disparaged the tactic, writing in a statement that “With this rescissions package, the Trump administration is illegally stripping nearly $1 billion in critical funding that supports kids, K-12 students, small businesses, and health and clean air research.” Schumer added that Senate Democrats will “challenge Trump’s illegal cuts.” The White House listed the programs that it rejected funding for, writing that tax dollars were being “wasted.” The programs included funding for several nongovernmental organizations that serve immigrants and refugees, NGOs that provide housing counseling, and funding that supports bringing foreign students and faculty to U.S. academic institutions. The administration also said it rejected funding for the Community Relations Services, a subagency of the Justice Department that was established as part of the Civil Rights Act and nicknamed “America’s Peacemaker.” The White House also listed denying funds for a program that grants debt relief to countries that implement climate change policies and a program that assists minority business owners. There were also funds rejected for what the White House deemed “overfunded and unaligned” HHS research programs. It also returned funds for the department’s Office of Minority Health. Trump used the same tactic to announce $4.9 billion in cuts last year, including $3.2 billion in cuts to USAID, $322 million in cuts for the USAID’s State Democracy fund and hundreds of millions of dollars from funding meant to support worldwide peacekeeping activities. The $4.9 billion foreign aid cuts were challenged in court last year, but the Supreme Court ultimately ruled in favor of the administration in September 2025. Congress approved a rescissions package in July 2025 that nixed $9 billion in foreign aid and for the Corporation of Public Broadcasting, which funds NPR and PBS. Last year, lawyers for the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan federal agency, wrote a post on WatchBlog that stated pocket rescissions are illegal. “A pocket rescission could allow a president to avoid spending the money regardless of whether Congress approves the rescission request,” the post said. “This would cede Congress’s power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds.” In its arguments, the Trump administration has cited the Impoundment Control Act, which Congress passed in 1974 with the aim of regulating the president’s control over the budget. It came after former President Richard Nixon had sought to withhold spending on programs that he did not support. The administration argues that it can withhold money through pocket rescissions, which had not been used in nearly 50 years until Trump revived them last year. Despite the tactic’s controversy, the White House again touted the president’s use of it Friday. “Last year, President Trump took the historic step of utilizing long-neglected Presidential authorities provided to him under the Impoundment Control Act to deploy the first ‘pocket rescission’ in 50 years,” the statement said, adding, “This year, he is continuing his commitment.”

articles.title: White House bars CNN from Air Force One for Trump’s upcoming trip
articles.summary: Real America’s Voice News replaces CNN on Air Force One amid escalating tensions between President Trump and US media.
articles.body:
CNN has been barred from flying on Air Force One to cover President Donald Trump on behalf of major television networks, the latest media restriction by the White House.

CNN was replaced by Real America’s Voice News, a conservative outlet, for the president’s trip to attend a college football game in Knoxville, Tennessee, according to White House guidance.

Last week, Trump announced he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds.

The White House press pool consists of five major broadcast outlets that take turns recording and distributing video. In a show of solidarity, the other four providers – Fox, ABC, CBS and NBC – declined to participate in the pool until access was restored.

The three barred news outlets responded to Trump’s ban with a lawsuit alleging the White House violated their First Amendment rights.

“Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference,” their statement said.

US District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily struck down the ban in an overnight ruling early on Thursday, saying the government’s argument lacked “factual support” for the claim that the outlets were barred to protect national security.

“Defendants offer no declarations or other support – classified or unclassified – explaining how any of the reporting they identified in their letters to Plaintiffs damaged the national security,” Kelly said in the ruling.

The judge’s decision addressed press passes to the White House and did not directly mention pool duties or Air Force One.

Earlier on Friday, the news outlets’ attorney Theodore Boutrous Jr said on CNN’s “The Lead with Jake Tapper” that the plaintiffs believe the judge’s ruling also covers the issue of pool access.

The spot on the presidential jet that was meant for CNN has long been reserved for a member of the US network video pool, which Real America’s Voice News is not a part of.
